lessons.title: Transaction Concept and ACID
lessons.concept: A transaction is a sequence of one or more SQL operations executed as a single logical unit of work. Transactions follow ACID properties: Atomicity (all or nothing), Consistency (valid state transitions), Isolation (concurrent transactions don't improperly interfere), and Durability (committed changes persist).
lessons.formula: COMMIT saves changes permanently. ROLLBACK undoes changes since transaction start/savepoint (DBMS-dependent behavior).
lessons.worked_example: Transferring money: debit account A and credit account B should either both succeed (COMMIT) or both be undone (ROLLBACK) if any step fails.
mistakes: Assuming partial success is acceptable in atomic operations
Thinking transactions are only for SELECT statements

lessons.title: COMMIT, ROLLBACK, and Savepoints
lessons.concept: COMMIT makes transaction changes permanent and visible according to isolation rules. ROLLBACK reverts uncommitted changes. Some DBMSs support savepoints to roll back to an intermediate point within a transaction without undoing the entire transaction.
lessons.formula: BEGIN/START TRANSACTION -> operations -> COMMIT or ROLLBACK. Savepoint (where supported): SAVEPOINT sp1; ROLLBACK TO sp1;
lessons.worked_example: START TRANSACTION; UPDATE accounts...; SAVEPOINT s1; UPDATE logs...; ROLLBACK TO s1; COMMIT; keeps account update but undoes log update after savepoint (if supported).
mistakes: Forgetting to COMMIT in environments without auto-commit
Assuming savepoint syntax/behavior is identical in every DBMS
Rolling back after commit (cannot undo committed transaction with ROLLBACK)
lessons.provenance: Authored original lesson; not scraped. Requires independent verification before TRUSTED promotion.

lessons.title: Concurrency and Isolation Basics
lessons.concept: When multiple transactions run concurrently, isolation levels control visibility of uncommitted/committed changes and phenomena like dirty reads, non-repeatable reads, and phantom reads. Higher isolation reduces anomalies but may reduce concurrency/performance.
lessons.formula: Common isolation levels (SQL standard): READ UNCOMMITTED, READ COMMITTED, REPEATABLE READ, SERIALIZABLE (availability/semantics vary by DBMS).
lessons.worked_example: At READ COMMITTED, a transaction does not see uncommitted changes from others, reducing dirty reads compared to READ UNCOMMITTED.
mistakes: Assuming all DBMSs implement isolation levels identically
Using highest isolation by default without considering performance trade-offs

practice.question: Which command permanently saves changes made in a transaction?
practice.explanation: COMMIT makes the transaction's changes permanent (durable) according to database rules.

practice.question: Which command undoes uncommitted transaction changes?
practice.explanation: ROLLBACK reverts changes made in the current transaction that have not been committed.

practice.question: Atomicity in ACID means:

options.B: All operations in a transaction succeed or none are applied
options.D: Only one user can access database

practice.explanation: Atomicity ensures the transaction is treated as an indivisible unit: either fully completed (commit) or fully undone (rollback).

practice.question: Durability in ACID refers to:

options.B: Committed changes persist even after failures

practice.explanation: Durability guarantees that once a transaction is committed, its changes survive subsequent system failures.

questions.explanation: Consistency ensures transactions preserve database integrity constraints/rules, moving the database between valid states.

questions.question: After a transaction is committed, issuing ROLLBACK will:

options.B: Not undo the committed transaction (it is already permanent)

questions.explanation: ROLLBACK affects uncommitted changes in the current transaction; once committed, changes are durable and cannot be reverted by ROLLBACK.
